Chart system concept 02

Register

Register leads with the numbers. Every chart sits in the same frame, so a reader learns its parts once: evidence label, title, measure line, figure, notes, source and table. Under or beside each figure, a register sets out the figures a reader would look up, with tabular figures, quiet rules and an order that answers the question. Prussian and Verdigris carry the data, with Stone for context and Charcoal for the subject a title names.

Chart system concept 02 · Register

On Charcoal

Two specimens on Charcoal: a line and a register. Newsprint carries the subject and the text. The palette lab found that Prussian and Verdigris, lifted the same amount, land only 0.022 apart in lightness here, so Register lifts them unequally: Verdigris 4% toward Newsprint and Prussian 66%. The pair then sits 0.13 apart in lightness and keeps its grayscale order, and every count is still printed. Pillar Red measures 4.49:1 on Charcoal and needs no keyline.

Chart system concept 02 · Register

Social card

Specimen S01 as a portrait post at 1080 by 1350 pixels, the size Instagram and LinkedIn use. It is live type at true size, so the box below scrolls on a phone. The card keeps the frame: evidence label, title, measure line, the party register, the dated votes and the full source line.

Other views: White · Newsprint · Charcoal · System

Alt text for the exported image

A card from Oath & Action. Finding: Nearly nine in ten Republicans and Democrats favored a ban on stock trading by members of Congress. Bars show 88 percent of Democrats, 87 percent of Republicans and 86 percent of all registered voters, from a survey fielded May 19 to 30, 2023. The House passed a ban 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026; on September 30 the Senate voted 53 to 47 to take it up, short of the 60 votes it needed.

Rules for cards

  • Type keeps its system roles at card size: label 26 px, title 60 px, figures 68 px, party names 32 px, votes 28 px, source 20 px.
  • The source line prints whole on the card itself.
  • Party rows share one ink and print the party name.
  • The wordmark sits at the foot; it is the only red on the card.

Chart system concept 02 · Register

The system on one sheet

The rules a designer or a builder needs to make the next chart: the frame and its parts, the type, the marks, the palettes with measured contrast, the table rules, notes and sources, red, and a short guide for readers.

Other views: White · Newsprint · Charcoal · Social card

1The frame

Studio note · not part of the chart

S03 Ranked bar

Reader questionWho changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?

Why this formA ranked register answers "who" by grouping the instruments by who acted, and its direction columns let a reader read across a row and down a column.

Every figure uses the same ten parts in the same order, so a reader learns them once.

  1. Rule2 px Charcoal across the figure. It opens every figure and nothing else on the page uses it.
  2. Evidence labelInter 700, 13/18, capitals, 0.06em. The kind (Finding, Association, Estimate, Illustration), then the grade in words.
  3. TitleInter Tight 800, 28/32 (22/27 on phones). A sentence that states the finding, with a verb that matches the grade.
  4. Measure lineInter 400, 15/22, Deep Stone. Measure, unit, place and period; any cropped scale is said here.
  5. FigureThe chart or the register. Wide artboard at 866 px, a 560 px artboard below that, a 328 px artboard on phones.
  6. Note in the drawingInter 400 or 600, 13/16, joined to its data by a 1 px leader.
  7. NotesInter 400, 14/20, Deep Stone, numbered, above a quiet rule. What a reader needs to read the figure fairly.
  8. Source lineInter 400, 13/18, Deep Stone. Publisher, table, period, place, date retrieved, qualification.
  9. Table"Show the table": every value, the notes and the source, readable by a screen reader.
  10. Studio noteDashed box beside the figure, used in the guide only.

Grid: 12 columns at 1440 px with 64 px margins and 24 px gutters; the figure takes 866 px and the studio note the rest. On phones, 16 px margins, one column, the figure first.

2Type

Locked faces only: Inter Tight for titles and big figures, Inter for everything else, Lora Italic for quoted words only. Every number is tabular, every minus is the true minus (−), and nothing falls under 13 px.

3Marks

  • Bars start at zero; in-row bars share one scale per table, and every bar's value is printed.
  • Lines may start above zero only when the measure line says so. Missing years and method changes break the line.
  • Points sit on one straight scale per panel. Small multiples share one scale.
  • Units are 14 px squares, one per record. Solid means a direction, hollow means no change, hatched means mixed, dashed means pending.
  • Gridlines are horizontal hairlines with no ticks; the baseline at zero is Charcoal.
  • The unit prints once, on the top tick or the first label.

4Palettes, measured

Lab values come from the shared palette lab; Register's own tints (the quiet rule, the kept tint and the two Charcoal lifts) are mixed in OKLab from locked colors, each with one job. Contrast is WCAG 2 against the ground. Marks that carry meaning clear 3:1; light fills inside a scale sit under 3:1 only where every value is printed, a studio judgment.

The direction pair, Verdigris and Prussian on White, differs by OKLab distance 0.256 (0.258 under deuteranopia, 0.261 under protanopia, 0.239 under tritanopia). Stone and Verdigris never separate two categories alone.

Diverging scales never pair red with blue. Register tests candidate B, Prussian through the ground to Verdigris, in S06; candidate A, Stone through a neutral to Verdigris, stays with the other concepts for Gate 2. No US state map uses Prussian, so a blue state never reads as a party.

5Tables

  • Numbers sit right-aligned in tabular figures, with one count of decimals per column, so the decimal points align.
  • A change column prints its sign: +0.2, −3.7. Zero prints as 0 in Deep Stone; a missing value prints as words.
  • Column heads carry the unit, once: "Documented, %". Rows carry no unit.
  • Rules stay quiet: Charcoal under the head, a quiet tint between rows, Stone above a group, Charcoal above the total.
  • The default sort answers the question: ranked by value, grouped by who acted, or by date. Long tables let a reader re-sort.
  • A bar inside the row shows the shape; the printed figure carries the value.
  • On a phone each row reflows into labeled lines, so no table scrolls sideways.
  • Group and total rows carry their own counts in bold, and they sum.

6Notes and sources

  • A note inside the drawing does one job: names the record, explains an odd encoding, or gives a reader's scale.
  • Join a note to its data with a 1 px leader or a bracket. Never hide a note behind hover.
  • Notes under the figure say what the reader needs to read it fairly: revisions, breaks, coding rules, margins of error.
  • Label illustrative items beside the item. Titles say what the evidence supports and nothing more.

The source line keeps section 15 order. Shorten it only by dropping words; every fact stays.

  1. PublisherU.S. Census Bureau
  2. Title or tablePoverty in the United States: 2025 (P60-290), Table 8
  3. Observation period2009 to 2025
  4. GeographyUnited States
  5. Date retrievedRetrieved November 6, 2026
  6. QualificationFigures for 2019 to 2024 include the Bureau's August 2026 revision

7Red

"The wordmark's ampersand and the lockmark's lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon's red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline's ampersand uses the view's working red. The hinge divider's ampersand takes its surface's ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian."
Rule 05.3 (D2-01)

On a chart page red never encodes a series, a category, a grade or a scale. It may mark the one point a title names, and only when no error or ask holds the view's red. On the White and Newsprint views that point is S02's 2021 low; the Charcoal view repeats it. The two drawings below are guide specimens, so their red does not count.

The point the title names takes the view's red

Pillar Red on the 2021 point, 4.17:1 on White. On Newsprint it takes a 1 px Charcoal keyline.

An ask arrives, so the point steps down to Charcoal

Read how the 2021 credit was paid Illustrative ask

The step a reader can take now outranks the headline's point, so the button keeps the red and the point turns Charcoal at the same 5.5 px radius.

8How to read our charts

For readers, printed once in a report and linked from every chart.

  1. Start with the label. It says what kind of evidence the chart holds. A Finding is measured; an Estimate depends on assumptions.
  2. Read the title as the claim. It is one sentence, and its verb says how sure the evidence is.
  3. Check the measure line. It says what was counted, where and when, and whether the scale starts above zero.
  4. Find the darkest ink. It marks the series or the point the title names; lighter ink gives context.
  5. Look up the numbers. The register under each chart prints the figures, so nothing depends on reading a bar by eye.
  6. Read the notes and the source. They say what the figure leaves out and where the numbers came from.
  7. Open the table. "Show the table" holds every value behind the chart.

Data: Oath & Action, Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot of 2026-10-15; U.S. Census Bureau tables retrieved November 6, 2026; Ballotpedia, retrieved November 6, 2026. Every source line sits under its chart.
